performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
question: How does Vivaldi make cold audible through rhythm rather than a change of instruments?
intro: Winter begins with repeated notes that gather into shivering. Rapid violin figures cut across them as gusts of wind, while the returning orchestral music develops the sonnet’s stamping feet and chattering teeth.

sections.label: Refrain and stamping · approximate
sections.mNote: the returning refrain develops into the stamping figure

sections.label: E♭-major refrain · approximate

cues.title: The texture accumulates
cues.text: Repeated notes begin low in the strings, and the higher parts join in stages. When the violin line adds trills, the same pulse becomes less steady in colour: the score’s shivering image grows from small changes inside a repeated rhythm.
cues.evidence: Mutopia I, opening bars 1–11, gives staggered entries and repeated notes, with trills in the solo part. The opening remains relatively quiet through the report’s first half-minute: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

cues.title: Wind across the pulse
cues.text: The solo violin breaks into much faster figures. The contrast is not just speed: its runs range across registers while brief orchestral interruptions recall the repeated-note shivering.
cues.evidence: The score labels bar 12 Orrido Vento and writes demisemiquaver solo figures. The same-recording guide places this at about 0:38, also the report’s strongest boundary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Instructions in the parts
cues.text: The winter sonnet describes shivering, harsh wind, stamping feet and chattering teeth. Vivaldi links those images to the score with verbal labels, so the bodily actions belong to the work’s published programme.
cues.evidence: The sonnet and score annotations are reproduced and discussed in the movement analysis: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996.

cues.title: Solo motion over recurring figures
cues.text: The soloist’s rapid patterns continue against reminders of the refrain. Listen for the difference between a running line and a note insistently repeated: Vivaldi uses both to keep this episode moving.
cues.evidence: Mutopia bars 26–38 place the solo’s rapid notes against recalled figures and later tutti wind interruptions. The guide places the episode around 1:23.5–2:02; the report has changes at 1:26, 1:40 and 1:50: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Work beyond Venice
cues.text: Between 1718 and 1720 Vivaldi worked in Mantua for Prince Philip of Hesse-Darmstadt. His career moved between institutional music-making, aristocratic employment and the opera stage; Venice was its centre, not its only setting.
cues.evidence: The Pietà biography records the Mantua appointment and its 1718–1720 period: https://www.vivaldichurchvenice.com/en/biography-of-antonio-vivaldi. No claim is made here that Winter was composed there.

cues.title: Teeth in the notation
cues.text: The score labels this later episode “Batter li denti”: chattering teeth. Repeated short notes make the image specific without requiring the listener to identify a real-world sound effect.
cues.evidence: Mutopia first violin bar 47 carries Batter li denti over repeated semiquavers; the same-recording guide places the image from about 2:31.5: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351; https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

cues.title: Stamping closes the movement
cues.text: The ending keeps the more forceful stamping figure rather than replaying every detail of the opening shiver. The refrain can close the movement through one recognisable portion of its material.
cues.evidence: The score and commentary identify the final ritornello, bars 56–63, with the stamping portion. The guide starts it near 3:01; the report shows sustained high relative level through 3:20 before the abrupt final decay: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Rapid arpeggios replace repeated notes
transitions.how: The opening has moved from F minor towards C minor. The soloist takes over with rapid broken chords and register changes, while the orchestra interrupts with the earlier shivering rhythm. The contrast is in speed and distribution of the figures, not a new basic tempo.
transitions.evidence: The guide gives 0:38 for score bar 12; the report’s strongest novelty peak is also 0:38. The score identifies the wind and the interruptions: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: The pulse becomes more insistent
transitions.how: The wind solo returns to F minor and the strings resume the repeated-note refrain. Shorter note values then transform its pulse into stamping figures. The new action develops inside the refrain instead of requiring a separate theme with unrelated material.
transitions.evidence: The guide places the return near 0:58 and the stamping development near 1:11.5; report changes occur at 1:00 and 1:10. Score bars 18–26 connect those figures: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: The soloist runs beyond the refrain
transitions.how: The full-string stamping yields to a running solo line. Repeated figures and brief tutti interventions retain a connection with what has just been heard, while the harmony travels from F minor towards E♭ major.
transitions.evidence: The commentary locates bars 26–38 at approximately 1:23.5–2:02. The report marks a change at 1:26 and the later E♭-major-compatible region; the score supplies the tonal destination: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: A familiar rhythm in E♭ major
transitions.how: The solo passage reaches E♭ major and repeated orchestral figures return in that key. The refrain keeps its shivering and short-note motion but does not yet restore the full stamping pattern reserved for the close.
transitions.evidence: The source identifies score bars 38–44 and places the return near 2:02; the report has a strong boundary at 2:02. The form is established by notation, not by the feature peak alone: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: A solo leads into repeated semiquavers
transitions.how: The orchestra yields to the soloist before the chattering figure takes hold. Repeated semiquavers then run through changing harmony, passing beyond E♭ major and returning towards F minor. The bodily image is maintained by rhythmic repetition rather than by staying on one chord.
transitions.evidence: The guide gives about 2:20.5 for bar 44 and 2:31.5 for the teeth image at bar 47. The report shows renewed rapid activity around 2:30. The region is deliberately broader than an individual entrance: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: The stamping portion returns to close
transitions.how: The solo episode has regained F minor. The full strings take up the stamping material, with rapid repeated notes reinforcing its rhythmic drive. A fragment of the refrain is enough to supply the final return and cadence.
transitions.evidence: Score bars 56–63 and the commentary identify the final stamping ritornello. Its same-recording start is about 3:01, within the report’s rise to the loud 3:00–3:20 region: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

composer.epithet: A violinist and theatre composer who made the returning orchestral refrain organise a soloist’s changing keys, textures and physical risks.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a violinist at St Mark’s, Venice
Violin teacher at the Ospedale della Pietà from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; theatre work in Venice and other cities
More than 500 concertos; operas, sacred vocal music, sonatas and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Vivaldi was born in Venice, the son of a barber who became a professional violinist at St Mark’s. Giovanni Battista Vivaldi taught his son the violin and remained involved in his musical work. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, acquiring the nickname il prete rosso, the red priest, from his hair. He soon ceased regularly celebrating Mass, later explaining that a condition of tightness in the chest prevented him. He travelled extensively, taught and managed operatic productions.

In 1703 the Ospedale della Pietà appointed him violin teacher. The Pietà was a charitable institution that cared for abandoned children; its celebrated performing body consisted of girls and women whose training could continue into adult professional responsibility within the institution. Concerts and services attracted Venetian patrons and foreign visitors. Vivaldi’s employment was periodically renewed and sometimes interrupted, but the connection endured for decades. The players supplied a practical laboratory: a concerto could be written for a particular instrumental skill, tried in performance, and followed by another that changed the problem.
